# pretty_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty-hex/

## Expand description

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, and a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-simple_hex)Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = vec![222, 173, 190, 239, 202, 254, 32, 24];
assert_eq!(simple_hex(&v), format!("{}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

`de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18`[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-pretty_hex)Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(pretty_hex(&v), format!("{:?}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-config_hex)Example of `config_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let cfg = HexConfig {title: false, width: 8, group: 0, ..HexConfig::default() };
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(config_hex(&v, cfg), format!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg)));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg));
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pretty](https://docs.rs/trait.PrettyHex.html)- Hex
- Allows generates hex dumps to a formatter.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_hex.html)- hex
- Return a hexdump of `source`in specified format.
- [hex_](https://docs.rs/fn.hex_write.html)- write
- Write hex dump in specified format.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex.html)- hex
- Return a multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Write multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation to the writer.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex.html)- hex
- Returns a one-line hexdump of `source`grouped in default format without header and ASCII column.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Dump `source`as hex octets in default format without header and ASCII column to the`writer`.

# pretty-hex 0.4.2 - Docs.rs

# pretty-hex

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

## Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use *;
let v = vec!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18
```
## Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use *;
let v: & = &;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
## Example of `config_hex()`

```
use *;
let cfg = HexConfig ;
let v = &include_bytes!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
Inspired by [haskell's pretty-hex](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/pretty-hex-1.0).

# heapless - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/heapless/^0.9/

## Expand description

`static` friendly data structures that don’t require dynamic memory allocation

The core principle behind `heapless` is that its data structures are backed by a *static* memory
allocation. For example, you can think of `heapless::Vec` as an alternative version of
`std::Vec` with fixed capacity and that can’t be re-allocated on the fly (e.g. via `push`).

All `heapless` data structures store their memory allocation *inline* and specify their capacity
via their type parameter `N`. This means that you can instantiate a `heapless` data structure on
the stack, in a `static` variable, or even in the heap.

```
use heapless::Vec; // fixed capacity `std::Vec`
// on the stack
let mut xs: Vec<u8, 8> = Vec::new(); // can hold up to 8 elements
xs.push(42)?;
assert_eq!(xs.pop(), Some(42));
// in a `static` variable
static mut XS: Vec<u8, 8> = Vec::new();
let xs = unsafe { &mut XS };
xs.push(42)?;
assert_eq!(xs.pop(), Some(42));
// in the heap (though kind of pointless because no reallocation)
let mut ys: Box<Vec<u8, 8>> = Box::new(Vec::new());
ys.push(42)?;
assert_eq!(ys.pop(), Some(42));
```
Because they have fixed capacity `heapless` data structures don’t implicitly reallocate. This
means that operations like `heapless::Vec.push` are *truly* constant time rather than amortized
constant time with potentially unbounded (depends on the allocator) worst case execution time
(which is bad/unacceptable for hard real time applications).

`heapless` data structures don’t use a memory allocator which means no risk of an uncatchable
Out Of Memory (OOM) condition while performing operations on them. It’s certainly possible to
run out of capacity while growing `heapless` data structures, but the API lets you handle this
possibility by returning a `Result` on operations that may exhaust the capacity of the data
structure.

List of currently implemented data structures:

- `Arc`- `std::sync::Arc`but backed by a lock-free memory pool rather than- `[global_allocator]`.
- `Box`- `std::boxed::Box`but backed by a lock-free memory pool rather than- `[global_allocator]`.
- `Object`
- `BinaryHeap`
- `Deque`
- `HistoryBuf`
- `IndexMap`
- `IndexSet`
- `LinearMap`
- `SortedLinkedList`
- `String`
- `Vec`
- `mpmc::MpMcQueue`
- `spsc::Queue`

[§](https://docs.rs#zeroize-support)Zeroize Support

The `zeroize` feature enables secure memory wiping for the data structures via the [ zeroize](https://crates.io/crates/zeroize)
crate. Sensitive data can be properly erased from memory when no longer needed.

When zeroizing a container, all underlying memory (including unused portion of the containers) is overwritten with zeros, length counters are reset, and the container is left in a valid but empty state that can be reused.

Check the [documentation of the zeroize crate](https://docs.rs/zeroize/) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate does *not* have a Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) and may make use of language
features and API in the standard library available in the latest stable Rust version.

In other words, changes in the Rust version requirement of this crate are not considered semver breaking change and may occur in patch version releases.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [binary_](https://docs.rs/binary_heap/index.html)- heap
- A priority queue implemented with a binary heap.
- [c_](https://docs.rs/c_string/index.html)- string
- A fixed capacity `CString`

- A fixed capacity double-ended queue.
- [history_](https://docs.rs/history_buf/index.html)- buf
- A “history buffer”, similar to a write-only ring buffer of fixed length.
- [index_](https://docs.rs/index_map/index.html)- map
- A fixed-capacity hash table where the iteration order is independent of the hash of the keys.
- [index_](https://docs.rs/index_set/index.html)- set
- A fixed-capacity hash set where the iteration order is independent of the hash values.
- [linear_](https://docs.rs/linear_map/index.html)- map
- A fixed capacity map/dictionary that performs lookups via linear search.
- [mpmc](https://docs.rs/mpmc/index.html)- `portable-atomic`, or- `mpmc_large`and- `target_has_atomic=ptr`, or non-- `mpmc_large`and- `target_has_atomic=8`
- A fixed capacity multiple-producer, multiple-consumer (MPMC) lock-free queue.
- [pool](https://docs.rs/pool/index.html)- `arm_llsc`, or 32-bit and (- `target_has_atomic=64`or- `portable-atomic`), or 64-bit and (- `target_has_atomic=128`and- `nightly`, or- `portable-atomic`)
- Memory and object pools
- [sorted_](https://docs.rs/sorted_linked_list/index.html)- linked_ - list
- A fixed sorted priority linked list, similar to `BinaryHeap``push`,`pop`, etc.
- [spsc](https://docs.rs/spsc/index.html)- `portable-atomic`or- `target_has_atomic=ptr`or- `has_atomic_load_store`
- A fixed capacity single-producer, single-consumer (SPSC) lock-free queue.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- `Storage`trait defining how data is stored in a container.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)
- A fixed capacity `String`
- [vec](https://docs.rs/vec/index.html)
- A fixed capacity `Vec`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rship_sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rship-sync/4.0.0-canary.64/rship_sync/

## Expand description

Sync Value System

High-precision synchronized value distribution using hyphae cells. Runs in-process with a 240Hz master clock for value updates.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rship_sync::{context, ValueRunnerRegistry, SyncValueConfig};
use std::sync::Arc;
// Initialize (once at startup)
let registry = Arc::new(ValueRunnerRegistry::new());
context::init(registry);
// Create and watch values
rship_sync::ensure_value("my/value", &SyncValueConfig { value: 0.0, rate: 1.0, running: true }, 30.0);
let cell = rship_sync::watch_value("my/value");
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use clock::`- [TICK_INTERVAL](https://docs.rs/clock/constant.TICK_INTERVAL.html);
- `pub use commands::`- [DestroySyncValue](https://docs.rs/commands/struct.DestroySyncValue.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [clock](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html)
- High-precision master clock for synchronized value distribution.
- [commands](https://docs.rs/commands/index.html)
- Sync value commands.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- Global sync context for accessing the value registry from reports.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- `SyncValueEngine`— projects- `SyncValueRuntime`entity state into the local- `ValueRunnerRegistry`.
- [entities](https://docs.rs/entities/index.html)
- Sync-specific types.
- [heartbeat](https://docs.rs/heartbeat/index.html)
- `SyncValueHeartbeat`— periodic 1Hz re-emit of- `SetSyncValueRate`for every known- `SyncValueRuntime`entity.
- [local](https://docs.rs/local/index.html)
- Local-only sync-value mutators for callers that derive their value
deterministically per-peer from the binding-node graph (Speed, Clock,
Wave, Interval generators). These keys must NOT go through the
`EnsureSyncValue`command path — that would emit a peer-replicated`SyncValueRuntime`entity, and every peer that locally re-evaluates the same generator graph would race to upsert the same key with a different UUID, doubling/N-tupling entity counts forever.
- [reports](https://docs.rs/reports/index.html)
- Sync value reports.
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/runtime_entity/index.html)- entity
- `SyncValueRuntime`entity — peer-replicated runtime state for a sync value.
- [value_](https://docs.rs/value_runner/index.html)- runner
- Lock-free value runner using hyphae cells.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [link](https://docs.rs/fn.link.html)
- Force linking to ensure inventory registrations are collected.

# smooth_operator_server - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator-server)smooth-operator-server

The reference WebSocket service for smooth-operator. It speaks the
schema-driven protocol in `smooth-operator/spec/` over a smooth-operator-backed
knowledge-chat runtime, so the generated TypeScript / Go / .NET / Python
clients can connect and drive real LLM turns unmodified.

# rship_shared_schemas - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rship-shared-schemas/4.0.0-canary.64/rship_shared_schemas/

## Expand description

Shared schema registry.

Hosts the `WellKnownSchema` enum (a closed set of schemas every SDK knows
about) and the `SchemaRef` reference type used by `Action`, `Emitter`, and
comp-engine entities. Generated to every SDK via typegen so misspelled or
invented schema ids are unrepresentable at compile time.

See `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-30-comp-engine-design.md`
§ “Shared-Schemas Registry”.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use registry::`- [GetAllSchemas](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetAllSchemas.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetAllSchemasOutput](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetAllSchemasOutput.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetSchemaByVariant](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetSchemaByVariant.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetSchemaByVariantOutput](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetSchemaByVariantOutput.html);
- `pub use schema_ref::`- [SchemaRef](https://docs.rs/schema_ref/enum.SchemaRef.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [SchemaEntry](https://docs.rs/well_known/struct.SchemaEntry.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [SchemaSemantic](https://docs.rs/well_known/enum.SchemaSemantic.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [WellKnownSchema](https://docs.rs/well_known/enum.WellKnownSchema.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [schema_for](https://docs.rs/well_known/fn.schema_for.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [registry](https://docs.rs/registry/index.html)
- Server-side reports for inspecting the shared-schemas registry from the UI.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_ref/index.html)- ref
- Typed schema-reference enum used by Action, Emitter, and downstream
entities. Prefer `SchemaRef::WellKnown(...)`at call sites; reach for`SchemaRef::Custom(...)`only when no well-known schema fits the value.
- [well_](https://docs.rs/well_known/index.html)- known
- Well-known schema enum — the closed set of schemas rship core knows about.
Every variant has exactly one registered body. Adding a variant requires
extending the exhaustive match in `schema_for`; missing a variant fails to compile.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [link](https://docs.rs/fn.link.html)
- Touch this from `typegen`and other binaries to force the linker to keep the`inventory::submit!`registrations alive.

# smooth_operator_adapter_dynamodb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-dynamodb/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_dynamodb/

## Expand description

DynamoDB single-table [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the AWS-serverless backend.

This is the production DynamoDB implementation of the one storage seam (see
`docs/STORAGE.md`). One table, overloaded `PK`/`SK` + two GSIs serve every
access pattern (the keys live in [`keys`]):

- **OLTP**(conversations / participants / messages / sessions): async CRUD over- `aws-sdk-dynamodb`, with the- **same observable semantics**as the in-memory / Postgres baselines — conversation idempotency on- `(org, idempotencyKey)`via a conditional GSI item, external-id participant resolve via- `GSI1`, monotonic message sequencing (an atomic counter item) with cursor paging, session status/counts.
- **Checkpoints**:- `DynamoCheckpointStore`- `CheckpointStore`- `checkpoint`]).
- **Knowledge**:- `DynamoKnowledgeBase`- `s3-vectors`feature (see [- `knowledge`] / [- `s3vectors`]).

[§](https://docs.rs#single-table-key-design)Single-table key design

| Entity | PK | SK | GSI1PK |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conversation | `ORG#<org>` | `CONV#<convId>` | `IDEM#<org>#<key>`+`CONV#<id>` |
| Participant | `CONV#<convId>` | `PART#<partId>` | `EXTERNAL#<convId>#<extId>` |
| Message | `CONV#<convId>` | `MSG#<padded seq>#<id>` | `MSG#<id>` |
| Session | `CONV#<convId>` | `SESS#<sessionId>` | `SESSION#<sessionId>` |
| Checkpoint | `CKPT#<agentId>` | `<padded iteration>#<id>` | `CKPTID#<id>` |
| Knowledge | `KNOW#<org>` | `DOC#<docId>` | — |

Each conversation writes **two** GSI1 entries (one by-idempotency, one
by-id), so both `create_conversation` idempotency lookups and standalone
`get_conversation(id)` are single queries.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deterministic](https://docs.rs/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- Deterministic, network-free pseudo-embedder.
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoCheckpointStore.html)- Checkpoint - Store
- DynamoDB-backed checkpoint store. Cheap to clone (a `Client`+`Handle`+ table name behind`Arc`-able fields).
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoConnectorConfigStore.html)- Connector - Config - Store
- DynamoDB-backed `ConnectorConfigStore`
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoDbAdapter.html)- DbAdapter
- DynamoDB single-table storage adapter.
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoIndexingStore.html)- Indexing - Store
- DynamoDB-backed `IndexingStore`
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoKnowledgeBase.html)- Knowledge - Base
- DynamoDB-backed knowledge base. Cheap to clone.
- [Dynamo](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamoSettingsStore.html)- Settings - Store
- DynamoDB-backed `SettingsStore`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Input](https://docs.rs/enum.InputType.html)- Type
- Whether an embedding is for a document being stored or a search query.
- [Knowledge](https://docs.rs/enum.KnowledgeBackend.html)- Backend
- Which dense-retrieval backend the knowledge slice uses.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Default embedding dimension (Voyage `voyage-3-large`shape; mirrors smooai’s`knowledge_vectors embedding vector(1024)`).
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_TABLE_NAME.html)- TABLE_ - NAME
- Default table name when none is configured.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_INLINE_BLOB.html)- INLINE_ - BLOB
- Conservative inline-blob ceiling. DynamoDB’s hard item limit is 400 KB; we
trip earlier (~300 KB) to leave headroom for keys/metadata and to fail loud
*before*the SDK rejects the`PutItem`. Blobs above this must spill to S3.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Turn text into dense vectors. Implementations must return one vector per
input string, each of length `Embedder::dim`

# smooth_operator_adapter_postgres - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-postgres/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_postgres/

## Expand description

Postgres + pgvector [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the dogfood backend.

This is the production Postgres implementation of the one storage seam (see
`docs/STORAGE.md`). It mirrors the smooai monorepo’s schema so dogfooding is
a swap, not a rewrite:

- **OLTP**(conversations / participants / messages / sessions): async CRUD over a- `deadpool_postgres`
- **Checkpoints**: smooth-operator’s- `PostgresCheckpointStore`- *synchronous*r2d2-pooled store) constructed against the- **same database**— so the engine’s- `with_checkpoint_store`plugs straight in and agent state lives next to the conversations it belongs to.
- **Knowledge**: a pgvector-backed- `PgKnowledgeBase`- `tsvector`BM25 → Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Text→vector goes through the- `Embedder`- `DeterministicEmbedder`- `GatewayEmbedder`
- **Memory**: a pgvector-backed- `PgMemory`- `(organization_id, user_id)`like the TS- `['memories', orgId, userId]`store. Implements the core- `Memory`- `Embedder`

[§](https://docs.rs#sharing-one-database-between-the-async-pool-and-the-sync-checkpoint-store)Sharing one database between the async pool and the sync checkpoint store

The OLTP/knowledge slices need async (`tokio-postgres` + `deadpool`); the
checkpoint slice is a sync trait backed by an r2d2 pool inside
smooth-operator. Both are pointed at the **same  conn_str**: we build the
async deadpool from it for our own queries, and hand the

*same*string to

`PostgresCheckpointStore::connect`, which stands up its own small r2d2 pool
and `checkpoints` table in that database. Two pools, two driver stacks, one
Postgres — the tables coexist (ours from [`schema`], theirs from their own
`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deterministic](https://docs.rs/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- Deterministic, network-free pseudo-embedder.
- [Gateway](https://docs.rs/struct.GatewayEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings`embedder (the SmooAI LiteLLM gateway).
- [Gateway](https://docs.rs/struct.GatewayReranker.html)- Reranker
- Cross-encoder reranker over the SmooAI gateway’s `/v1/rerank`endpoint (feature gap G8).
- [Http](https://docs.rs/struct.HttpRerankBackend.html)- Rerank - Backend
- The real backend: a Cohere/Voyage-style `/v1/rerank`call over the gateway.
- [PgAgent](https://docs.rs/struct.PgAgentConfigResolver.html)- Config - Resolver
- Postgres-backed `AgentConfigResolver``agents`table.
- [PgConnector](https://docs.rs/struct.PgConnectorConfigStore.html)- Config - Store
- Postgres-backed `ConnectorConfigStore``connector_configs`.
- [PgIndexing](https://docs.rs/struct.PgIndexingStore.html)- Store
- Postgres-backed `IndexingStore``indexing_runs`.
- [PgKnowledge](https://docs.rs/struct.PgKnowledgeBase.html)- Base
- pgvector knowledge base. Cheap to clone (all fields are `Arc`/pool handles).
- [PgMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.PgMemory.html)
- pgvector-backed agent memory, bound to one `(organization_id, user_id)`namespace. Cheap to clone (all fields are`Arc`/pool handles + small strings).
- [PgSettings](https://docs.rs/struct.PgSettingsStore.html)- Store
- Postgres-backed `SettingsStore``agent_settings`.
- [Postgres](https://docs.rs/struct.PostgresAdapter.html)- Adapter
- Postgres + pgvector storage adapter.
- [Rerank](https://docs.rs/struct.RerankScore.html)- Score
- One scored candidate returned by a `RerankBackend``documents`array, and its relevance score against the query.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Input](https://docs.rs/enum.InputType.html)- Type
- Whether an embedding is for a document being stored or a search query.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Default embedding dimension (Voyage `voyage-3-large`shape; mirrors smooai’s`knowledge_vectors embedding vector(1024)`).
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_RERANK_MODEL.html)- RERANK_ - MODEL
- Default rerank model requested over the gateway (Cohere-compatible). Distinct from the embedding model and the chat model.
- [OPENAI_](https://docs.rs/constant.OPENAI_SMALL_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- SMALL_ - EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Dimension returned by OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Turn text into dense vectors. Implementations must return one vector per
input string, each of length `Embedder::dim`
- [Rerank](https://docs.rs/trait.RerankBackend.html)- Backend
- A pluggable rerank backend.

# smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_nats - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-backplane-nats/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_nats/

## Expand description

NATS [ Backplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/trait.Backplane.html) — cross-pod scale-out + a shared event bus.

Same shape as the Redis adapter (a per-pod [ InMemoryBackplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html) for local
registry + delivery, plus a bus for cross-pod fan-out) but over NATS subjects.
NATS is attractive here beyond raw fan-out: queue groups, JetStream
persistence/replay, and the fact that the same broker doubles as the
platform’s multi-channel event bus — so non-AI publishers (job status,
ingestion progress, notifications) and other services can share it.

Per call:

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Nats](https://docs.rs/struct.NatsBackplane.html)- Backplane
- A `Backplane``publish`out across pods over NATS.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_SUBJECT.html)- SUBJECT
- Default subject. Override via `NatsBackplane::connect_on_subject`

---

# smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-backplane-redis/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis/

## Expand description

Redis / Valkey [ Backplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/trait.Backplane.html) — the horizontal scale-out seam.

The default [ InMemoryBackplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html) only reaches sockets held by the current
process, so with more than one replica an event produced on pod A can’t reach
a socket on pod B.

[closes that gap](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)

`RedisBackplane`**without changing the trait or any call site**: it keeps a per-pod

[for the local registry + delivery, and adds a Redis pub/sub bus for cross-pod fan-out.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html)

`InMemoryBackplane`Per call:

- `attach`- `detach`- `associate`- **local**— a connection lives on exactly one pod, so only that pod registers it.
- `publish`- `BackplaneEnvelope`- `Target`- *its own*registry and delivers to its sockets — so the same- `publish`call fans out across the whole fleet. The origin pod skips its own echo (it already delivered).

This is the classic pub/sub fan-out (the shape Socket.IO’s Redis adapter uses): no shared connection registry, each pod authoritative for its own sockets.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Redis](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)- Backplane
- A `Backplane``publish`out across pods over Redis/Valkey pub/sub.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_CHANNEL.html)- CHANNEL
- Default pub/sub channel. Override via `RedisBackplane::connect_on_channel`

---

# smooth_operator_adapter_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-memory/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_memory/

## Expand description

In-memory [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the conformance / test baseline.

All OLTP slices (conversations, participants, messages, sessions) live in
`HashMap`s behind a single `RwLock`. The checkpoint and knowledge slices
delegate to smooth-operator’s own [ MemoryCheckpointStore](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/checkpoint/struct.MemoryCheckpointStore.html) and

[, which are exactly what the engine expects — so this adapter is a faithful (if non-durable) stand-in for Postgres/DynamoDB.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/knowledge/struct.InMemoryKnowledge.html)

`InMemoryKnowledge`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- In-memory storage adapter. Cheap to clone is *not*a goal — wrap in`Arc`for sharing.

# pretty-hex 0.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty-hex/0.4.2

# pretty-hex

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

## Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use *;
let v = vec!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18
```
## Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use *;
let v: & = &;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
## Example of `config_hex()`

```
use *;
let cfg = HexConfig ;
let v = &include_bytes!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
Inspired by [haskell's pretty-hex](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/pretty-hex-1.0).

---

# pretty_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty-hex/0.4.2/target-redirect/pretty_hex/

## Expand description

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, and a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-simple_hex)Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = vec![222, 173, 190, 239, 202, 254, 32, 24];
assert_eq!(simple_hex(&v), format!("{}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

`de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18`[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-pretty_hex)Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(pretty_hex(&v), format!("{:?}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-config_hex)Example of `config_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let cfg = HexConfig {title: false, width: 8, group: 0, ..HexConfig::default() };
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(config_hex(&v, cfg), format!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg)));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg));
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pretty](https://docs.rs/trait.PrettyHex.html)- Hex
- Allows generates hex dumps to a formatter.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_hex.html)- hex
- Return a hexdump of `source`in specified format.
- [hex_](https://docs.rs/fn.hex_write.html)- write
- Write hex dump in specified format.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex.html)- hex
- Return a multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Write multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation to the writer.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex.html)- hex
- Returns a one-line hexdump of `source`grouped in default format without header and ASCII column.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Dump `source`as hex octets in default format without header and ASCII column to the`writer`.

# pretty_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty-hex/0.4.2/pretty_hex/index.html

## Expand description

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, and a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-simple_hex)Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = vec![222, 173, 190, 239, 202, 254, 32, 24];
assert_eq!(simple_hex(&v), format!("{}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

`de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18`[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-pretty_hex)Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(pretty_hex(&v), format!("{:?}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-config_hex)Example of `config_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let cfg = HexConfig {title: false, width: 8, group: 0, ..HexConfig::default() };
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(config_hex(&v, cfg), format!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg)));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg));
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pretty](https://docs.rs/trait.PrettyHex.html)- Hex
- Allows generates hex dumps to a formatter.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_hex.html)- hex
- Return a hexdump of `source`in specified format.
- [hex_](https://docs.rs/fn.hex_write.html)- write
- Write hex dump in specified format.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex.html)- hex
- Return a multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Write multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation to the writer.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex.html)- hex
- Returns a one-line hexdump of `source`grouped in default format without header and ASCII column.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Dump `source`as hex octets in default format without header and ASCII column to the`writer`.

## Expand description

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, and a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

println!("{}", v.hex_dump());
```

`de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18`[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-pretty_hex)Example of `pretty_hex()`

# pretty-hex 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty-hex/0.4.1

# pretty-hex

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

## Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use *;
let v = vec!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18
```
## Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use *;
let v: & = &;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
## Example of `config_hex()`

```
use *;
let cfg = HexConfig ;
let v = &include_bytes!;
assert_eq!;
println!;
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
Inspired by [haskell's pretty-hex](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/pretty-hex-1.0).

# pretty_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty-hex

## Expand description

A Rust library providing pretty hex dump.

A `simple_hex()` way renders one-line hex dump, and a `pretty_hex()` way renders
columned multi-line hex dump with addressing and ASCII representation.
A `config_hex()` way renders hex dump in specified format.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-simple_hex)Example of `simple_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = vec![222, 173, 190, 239, 202, 254, 32, 24];
assert_eq!(simple_hex(&v), format!("{}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

`de ad be ef  ca fe 20 18`[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-pretty_hex)Example of `pretty_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(pretty_hex(&v), format!("{:?}", v.hex_dump()));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_dump());
```
Output:

```
Length: 30 (0x1e) bytes
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3  af 03 d2 1e  7e 73 ba c8  bd 84 0f 83   kN......~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90  23 67 4b 48  db b1 bc 35  bf ee         ....#gKH...5..
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-config_hex)Example of `config_hex()`

```
use pretty_hex::*;
let cfg = HexConfig {title: false, width: 8, group: 0, ..HexConfig::default() };
let v = &include_bytes!("../tests/data");
assert_eq!(config_hex(&v, cfg), format!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg)));
println!("{:?}", v.hex_conf(cfg));
```
Output:

```
0000:   6b 4e 1a c3 af 03 d2 1e   kN......
0008:   7e 73 ba c8 bd 84 0f 83   ~s......
0010:   89 d5 cf 90 23 67 4b 48   ....#gKH
0018:   db b1 bc 35 bf ee         ...5..
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pretty](https://docs.rs/trait.PrettyHex.html)- Hex
- Allows generates hex dumps to a formatter.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_hex.html)- hex
- Return a hexdump of `source`in specified format.
- [hex_](https://docs.rs/fn.hex_write.html)- write
- Write hex dump in specified format.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex.html)- hex
- Return a multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Write multi-line hexdump in default format complete with addressing, hex digits, and ASCII representation to the writer.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex.html)- hex
- Returns a one-line hexdump of `source`grouped in default format without header and ASCII column.
- [simple_](https://docs.rs/fn.simple_hex_write.html)- hex_ - write
- Dump `source`as hex octets in default format without header and ASCII column to the`writer`.

# bytes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytes/^1/

## Expand description

Provides abstractions for working with bytes.

The `bytes` crate provides an efficient byte buffer structure
([ Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)) and traits for working with buffer
implementations (

[,](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.Buf.html)

`Buf`[).](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.BufMut.html)

`BufMut`[§](https://docs.rs#bytes)`Bytes`

`Bytes` is an efficient container for storing and operating on contiguous
slices of memory. It is intended for use primarily in networking code, but
could have applications elsewhere as well.

`Bytes` values facilitate zero-copy network programming by allowing multiple
`Bytes` objects to point to the same underlying memory. This is managed by
using a reference count to track when the memory is no longer needed and can
be freed.

A `Bytes` handle can be created directly from an existing byte store (such as `&[u8]`
or `Vec<u8>`), but usually a `BytesMut` is used first and written to. For
example:

```
use bytes::{BytesMut, BufMut};
let mut buf = BytesMut::with_capacity(1024);
buf.put(&b"hello world"[..]);
buf.put_u16(1234);
let a = buf.split();
assert_eq!(a, b"hello world\x04\xD2"[..]);
buf.put(&b"goodbye world"[..]);
let b = buf.split();
assert_eq!(b, b"goodbye world"[..]);
assert_eq!(buf.capacity(), 998);
```
In the above example, only a single buffer of 1024 is allocated. The handles
`a` and `b` will share the underlying buffer and maintain indices tracking
the view into the buffer represented by the handle.

See the [struct docs](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#buf-bufmut)`Buf`, `BufMut`

These two traits provide read and write access to buffers. The underlying
storage may or may not be in contiguous memory. For example, `Bytes` is a
buffer that guarantees contiguous memory, but a [rope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rope_(data_structure)) stores the bytes in
disjoint chunks. `Buf` and `BufMut` maintain cursors tracking the current
position in the underlying byte storage. When bytes are read or written, the
cursor is advanced.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-with-read-and-write)Relation with `Read` and `Write`

At first glance, it may seem that `Buf` and `BufMut` overlap in
functionality with [ std::io::Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html) and

[. However, they serve different purposes. A buffer is the value that is provided as an argument to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write``Read::read` and `Write::write`. `Read` and `Write` may then
perform a syscall, which has the potential of failing. Operations on `Buf`
and `BufMut` are infallible.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buf](https://docs.rs/buf/index.html)
- Utilities for working with buffers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)
- A cheaply cloneable and sliceable chunk of contiguous memory.
- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.BytesMut.html)- Mut
- A unique reference to a contiguous slice of memory.
- [TryGet](https://docs.rs/struct.TryGetError.html)- Error
- Error type for the `try_get_`methods of`Buf``Buf``try_get_`methods.

# defmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/defmt/^1.0.1/

## Expand description

A highly efficient logging framework that targets resource-constrained devices, like microcontrollers.

Check out the defmt book at [https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com](https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com) for more
information about how to use it.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `defmt` wire format might change between minor versions. Attempting to
read a defmt stream with an incompatible version will result in an error,
and any tool used to process that stream should first check for a symbol
named like `_defmt_version_ = X`, where X indicates the wire format version
in use.

Updating your version of defmt might mean you also have to update your
version of `defmt-print` or `defmt-decoder`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert](https://docs.rs/macro.assert.html)
- Just like the `core::assert!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Just like the `core::assert_eq!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Just like the `core::assert_ne!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html)
- Generates a bitflags structure that can be formatted with defmt.
- [dbg](https://docs.rs/macro.dbg.html)
- Just like the `std::dbg!``defmt`is used to log the message at`TRACE`level.
- [debug](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)
- Logs data at *debug*level.
- [debug_](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_assert.html)- assert
- Just like the `core::debug_assert!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [debug_](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Just like the `core::debug_assert_eq!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [debug_](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Just like the `core::debug_assert_ne!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [error](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)
- Logs data at *error*level.
- [expect](https://docs.rs/macro.expect.html)
- This is an alias for defmt’s `unwrap`
- [info](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)
- Logs data at *info*level.
- [intern](https://docs.rs/macro.intern.html)
- Creates an interned string (`Str`
- [panic](https://docs.rs/macro.panic.html)
- Just like the `core::panic!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [println](https://docs.rs/macro.println.html)
- Always logs data irrespective of log level.
- [timestamp](https://docs.rs/macro.timestamp.html)
- Defines the global timestamp provider for defmt.
- [todo](https://docs.rs/macro.todo.html)
- Just like the `core::todo!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [trace](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)
- Logs data at *trace*level.
- [unimplemented](https://docs.rs/macro.unimplemented.html)
- Just like the `core::unimplemented!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [unreachable](https://docs.rs/macro.unreachable.html)
- Just like the `core::unreachable!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)
- Unwraps an `Option`or`Result`, panicking if it is`None`or`Err`.
- [warn](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)
- Logs data at *warn*level.
- [write](https://docs.rs/macro.write.html)
- Writes formatted data to a `Formatter`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Debug2](https://docs.rs/struct.Debug2Format.html)- Format
- An “adapter” type to feed `Debug`values into defmt macros, which expect`defmt::Format`values.
- [Display2](https://docs.rs/struct.Display2Format.html)- Format
- An “adapter” type to feed `Display`values into defmt macros, which expect`defmt::Format`values.
- [Encoder](https://docs.rs/struct.Encoder.html)
- Encode raw defmt frames for sending over the wire.
- [Formatter](https://docs.rs/struct.Formatter.html)
- Handle to a defmt logger.
- [Str](https://docs.rs/struct.Str.html)
- An interned string created via `intern!`

- Block until host has read all pending data.

# embedded_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/embedded-io/^0.7/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#embedded-io)`embedded-io`

This project is developed and maintained by the [HAL team](https://github.com/rust-embedded/wg#the-hal-team).

Input/Output traits for embedded systems.

Rust’s `std::io` traits are not available in `no_std` targets, mainly because `std::io::Error`
requires allocation. This crate contains replacement equivalent traits, usable in `no_std`
targets.

[§](https://docs.rs#differences-with-stdio)Differences with `std::io`

- `Error`is an associated type. This allows each implementor to return its own error type, while avoiding- `dyn`or- `Box`. This is consistent with how errors are handled in- `embedded-hal`
- In `std::io`, the`Read`/`Write`traits might be blocking or non-blocking (i.e. returning`WouldBlock`errors) depending on the file descriptor’s mode, which is only known at run-time. This allows passing a non-blocking stream to code that expects a blocking stream, causing unexpected errors. To solve this,`embedded-io`specifies`Read`/`Write`are always blocking, and adds new`ReadReady`/`WriteReady`traits to allow using streams in a non-blocking way.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-cargo-features)Optional Cargo features

- `std`- `From`impls to convert to/from- `std::io`structs.
- `alloc`- `Box`, adds- `Write`impl to- `Vec`.
- `defmt`- `defmt::Format`from- `defmt`1.x for enums and structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.81 and up. It *might*
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

See [here](https://docs.rs/docs/msrv.md) for details on how the MSRV may be upgraded.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- Possible kinds of errors.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/enum.ReadExactError.html)- Exact - Error
- Error returned by `Read::read_exact`
- [Seek](https://docs.rs/enum.SeekFrom.html)- From
- Enumeration of possible methods to seek within an I/O object.
- [Slice](https://docs.rs/enum.SliceWriteError.html)- Write - Error
- Errors that could be returned by `Write`on`&mut [u8]`.
- [Write](https://docs.rs/enum.WriteFmtError.html)- FmtError
- Error returned by `Write::write_fmt`

# hash32 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hash32/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

32-bit hashing algorithms

[§](https://docs.rs#why)Why?

Because 32-bit architectures are a thing (e.g. ARM Cortex-M) and you don’t want your hashing function to pull in a bunch of slow 64-bit compiler intrinsics (software implementations of 64-bit operations).

[§](https://docs.rs#relationship-to-corehash)Relationship to `core::hash`

This crate extends [ core::hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/hash/index.html) with a 32-bit version of

`Hasher`, which extends
`core::hash::Hasher`. It requires that the hasher only performs 32-bit operations when computing
the hash, and adds [to get the hasher’s result as a](https://docs.rs/trait.Hasher.html#tymethod.finish32)

`finish32``u32`. The standard `finish`
method should just zero-extend this result.Since it extends `core::hash::Hasher`, `Hasher` can be used with any type which implements the
standard `Hash` trait.

This crate also adds a version of `BuildHasherDefault` with a const constructor, to work around
the `core` version’s lack of one.

[§](https://docs.rs#hashers)Hashers

This crate provides implementations of the following 32-bit hashing algorithms:

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-code)Generic code

In generic code, the trait bound `H: core::hash::Hasher` accepts *both* 64-bit hashers like
`std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher`; and 32-bit hashers like the ones defined in this
crate (`hash32::FnvHasher` and `hash32::Murmur3Hasher`)

The trait bound `H: hash32::Hasher` is *more* restrictive as it only accepts 32-bit hashers.

The `BuildHasherDefault<H>` type implements the `core::hash::BuildHasher` trait so it can
construct both 32-bit and 64-bit hashers. To constrain the type to only produce 32-bit hasher
you can add the trait bound `H::Hasher: hash32::Hasher`

[§](https://docs.rs#msrv)MSRV

This crate is guaranteed to compile on latest stable Rust. It *might* compile on older
versions but that may change in any new patch release.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildHasherDefault.html)- Hasher - Default
- A copy of `core::hash::BuildHasherDefault`
- [FnvHasher](https://docs.rs/struct.FnvHasher.html)
- 32-bit Fowler-Noll-Vo hasher
- [Murmur3](https://docs.rs/struct.Murmur3Hasher.html)- Hasher
- 32-bit MurmurHash3 hasher

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Hasher](https://docs.rs/trait.Hasher.html)
- An extension of [core::hash::Hasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/hash/trait.Hasher.html)for hashers which use 32 bits.
